It’s a fragment of coastline on an island off West Timor, which itself is a far-flung extremity of the eastern Indonesian archipelago, closer to Darwin than Jakarta. Aussie surfers started coming here 40-odd years ago, arriving for Rote’s long, clean waves, magicked up by a rare blend of wind, swell, and bathymetry.

There are other elements that give Rote its dream-come-true energy: tropical weather, white sand beaches, dense fringes of coconut palms, lingering sunsets, a steady trade wind in the dry season that keeps the mosquitoes down. Rote is, alluringly, always on island time. Crucially, it’s not easy to reach—good for surfers who don’t much like sharing a wave. The long journey to get here is why Rote has stayed Rote, one of the most wonderfully inconvenient places out there.

Amid all this remoteness, the first top-end resort has just opened, Nihi Rote and Hospitality Academy, sister property to Nihi Sumba, west of here. Both these hotels—a few hundred miles apart—front one of the most coveted waves in the world. When I visit, the hotel is still taking shape. At the eastern end of the bay is a clutch of thoughtfully designed, thatched, low-rise villas, each with a swimming pool; the interiors in mine use local materials such as lontar palm and ikat textiles. The gathering place is beach club Nammo, with its poolside restaurant and watersports instructors, smack in front of Bo’a break. Here I wait for the tide to turn before paddling out. When Nihi Rote launches fully in October, there will be 21 villas, three pools, a spa, a pump track, and a golf simulator. It is also planning to build and sell multimillion-dollar residences alongside the property.

One night, I’m invited to Rote Hospitality Academy, where Timorese trainees have prepared an endearing evening of traditional song and dance; storytelling; and a feast of coconut rice with lemongrass, rendang beef stew, and grilled fish with sambal. Sitting around the fire pit, toes in the sand, the students share stories with me about the cuisine; traditional string instrument sasando, made of bamboo; and their struggles with learning to swim. For many, it is their first job, or their first job in hospitality, and it’s been a fast-track whirlwind. Before the hotel opened, they had already hosted a big-splash 50th birthday party for its owner, Michael Schwab, son of investment firm founder Charles Schwab. “We’ve never seen anything like this on Rote,” says one student.

blocks.x: Change is not always easy, especially in a place that, until recently, relied on seaweed farming and fishing. I feel a pang as I drive past Rote’s cinder-block and tin-roof huts, women on the porch pausing to wave as they plait each other’s hair, sepia-tinged frangipani blossoms strewn on the ground. Rote has long been open to outsiders—and that is increasingly rare in this world of ours. “Do you live here?” is a regular refrain from locals as I freewheel around town. It is always uttered with a smile—on the harbor, at a café, down on the beach. When I reply that I am passing through, they say: Come and live here, you are welcome, bring your family. Many have taken up such invitations, seduced by the island’s stress-free, go-slow rhythm. “We were also passing through,” a South African surfer tells me, echoing my line. “But that was two years ago.” He and his partner have had a baby, bought some land, and are now building a cottage.
